growing higher" According to an Associated

the worlds loftiest peak would double its present
height-29,000 feet-in 145 centuries, relatively
short period of time geologically speaking.


But it is unlikely that there will be any such
pushing up OF the great Asian hills. The power
to force them higher must be either volcanic or
oceanic. Vast subterranean explosions could
occur, opening tremendous craters in Tibet; but
DR.. Kirshnan does not anticipate any develop
ment of that kind. The more important dynamic
element of the prevailing era in the earth's
history is that of the weight of water. If the
world grows warmer and the ice of the polar
zones mets, the seas will become heavier. This
circumstance would have the effect of squeezing
the Himalayas upward. 1t also would lift the
Rockies, the Andes, the Apennines and many
other ranges, including particularly the noun
talns of Japan.


Evidence in support of the theory referred to
may be found in the gradual shortening of the
glaciers of Switzerland. George Gamow in his
biography of the Earth" dramatzes what ap-

and moves little. Each swapping means an

condition of torridity supplanting the present
cold Of the Arctic and the Antarctic, the lifting
OF the worlds mountains eventually must halt.
That is what has occurred in the Laurentians of
Canada and our own Appalachians.
